subject: physics

items.q: Light from a distant galaxy is compared with light from the same element produced in a laboratory on Earth. What is observed about the light from the galaxy?
items.correct: Its wavelength is longer than the laboratory value
items.misconception: Its wavelength is shorter than the value on Earth
items.why: Students remember that recession changes the wave but picture the waves being bunched up rather than stretched out, and shift is remembered without its direction. A receding source stretches the waves reaching the observer, so the wavelength increases. The specification defines red-shift as an observed increase in wavelength, and longer wavelength lies towards the red end.
items.random_wrong: It looks red instead of its normal colour

items.q: The light from galaxy B shows a bigger observed increase in wavelength than the light from galaxy A. What can be concluded about galaxy B?
items.correct: It is further away than A and is moving faster
items.misconception: It is moving faster, but its distance is unknown
items.why: Everyday experience of objects slowing down as they travel is applied to galaxies, which reverses the relationship the specification gives. The specification states the opposite: the further away the galaxies, the faster they are moving and the bigger the observed increase in wavelength. Speed rises with distance rather than falling.
items.random_wrong: It is nearer than A and is moving more slowly

items.q: The light from most distant galaxies shows red-shift. What does this observation provide evidence for?
items.correct: That space itself, the universe, is expanding
items.misconception: That the galaxies fly out through existing space
items.why: The word bang brings a firework or a bomb to mind, and every explosion a student has seen happens inside a room or a sky that already exists. The observed red-shift is evidence that space itself is expanding, so the galaxies are carried apart by the growth of space rather than travelling through a pre-existing space.
items.random_wrong: That the Earth sits at the centre of the universe

items.q: According to the Big Bang theory, what was the universe like at the very beginning?
items.correct: A very small region, extremely hot and dense
items.misconception: A huge cold cloud that later heated up and shrank
items.why: Supernovae appear in the same section of the specification, and both are described with the word explosion, so the two are merged. A supernova is one star exploding within a universe that already exists. The Big Bang theory describes the beginning of the universe itself, from a very small, extremely hot and dense region.
items.random_wrong: A single giant star that exploded out into space

items.q: What do observations of supernovae made since 1998 onwards suggest about distant galaxies?
items.correct: They are receding ever faster as time goes on
items.misconception: They are gradually slowing as they recede
items.why: Thrown objects always slow down, so an expansion that started long ago is expected to be losing speed by now. The specification states the opposite: since 1998 onwards, observations of supernovae suggest that distant galaxies are receding ever faster.
items.random_wrong: They are receding at one steady, fixed speed

items.q: Every distant galaxy is observed to be receding, and the further away a galaxy is the faster it recedes. Why is this evidence that the universe is expanding?
items.correct: Because space between all the galaxies is stretching
items.misconception: Because the galaxies were thrown outwards through space
items.why: The word bang brings a firework or a bomb to mind, and every explosion a student has seen happens inside a room or a sky that already exists. The observed red-shift is evidence that space itself is expanding, so the galaxies are carried apart by the growth of space rather than travelling through a pre-existing space.
items.random_wrong: Because the Earth must be at the centre of it all

items.q: How does the observed red-shift provide evidence for the Big Bang model?
items.correct: An expanding universe must once have been small and dense
items.misconception: The stretched light is left over from the original explosion
items.why: The word bang brings a firework or a bomb to mind, and every explosion a student has seen happens inside a room or a sky that already exists. The observed red-shift is evidence that space itself is expanding, so the galaxies are carried apart by the growth of space rather than travelling through a pre-existing space.
items.random_wrong: It proves the Big Bang, so the theory can never be changed

items.q: Which statement best describes how scientists were able to use observations to arrive at the Big Bang theory?
items.correct: A model was proposed to explain what was observed
items.misconception: The theory came first and observations were chosen to fit
items.why: Proof is treated as the goal of science, so strong supporting evidence is read as closing the question for good. Scientists use observations to arrive at theories, and those theories are tested against further observations. The supernova observations made since 1998 onwards changed what is said about the expansion, which shows that a theory can still develop.
items.random_wrong: Nobody saw the beginning, so the theory is untestable

items.q: Which statement about dark mass and dark energy matches what the specification says?
items.correct: They are examples of what is still not understood
items.misconception: They are fully explained by the Big Bang theory
items.why: Anything that has a name and appears in a specification is assumed to be a settled piece of knowledge. The specification states that there is still much about the universe that is not understood, for example dark mass and dark energy. Naming something is not the same as explaining it.
items.random_wrong: They both name the same invisible material

items.q: The pattern of lines in the spectrum of a distant galaxy is compared with the pattern produced by the same element on Earth. What is observed?
items.correct: The lines are all shifted towards the red end
items.misconception: The lines are shifted towards the blue end
items.why: The idea of waves being pushed ahead of a moving source is half remembered, and the pushing is imagined as stretching rather than compressing. Waves ahead of an approaching source are compressed, giving a shorter wavelength. The specification links the observed increase in wavelength to galaxies that are receding.
items.random_wrong: The whole galaxy appears red rather than white

items.q: Light from galaxies X, Y and Z is examined. X shows a small increase in wavelength, Y a medium increase and Z a large increase. Which galaxy is furthest away?
items.correct: Z, because it shows the biggest increase
items.misconception: X, because it shows the smallest increase
items.why: Everyday experience of objects slowing down as they travel is applied to galaxies, which reverses the relationship the specification gives. The specification states the opposite: the further away the galaxies, the faster they are moving and the bigger the observed increase in wavelength. Speed rises with distance rather than falling.
items.random_wrong: Y, because a medium shift means a mid distance

items.q: Observations of supernovae made since 1998 onwards changed what scientists say about the expansion of the universe. What does this show about scientific theories?
items.correct: New observations can change an accepted theory
items.misconception: A theory becomes a fact once the evidence supports it
items.why: Proof is treated as the goal of science, so strong supporting evidence is read as closing the question for good. Scientists use observations to arrive at theories, and those theories are tested against further observations. The supernova observations made since 1998 onwards changed what is said about the expansion, which shows that a theory can still develop.
items.random_wrong: Theories about the distant past can never be tested

items.q: A galaxy shows a large red-shift. Does it look red?
items.correct: No. Red-shift means the wavelength of its light has increased, so lines in its spectrum sit nearer the red end than the laboratory lines do.
items.misconception: Red-shift means the galaxy has turned red, so a red-shifted galaxy looks red and a galaxy that does not look red is not red-shifted.
items.why: The name contains a colour, and the only shift a student has met before is a change of colour, so the term is read as a description of appearance. The evidence is the position of lines in a spectrum, not the overall colour. The whole pattern from a known element is found at longer wavelengths than the laboratory pattern, and that movement towards the red end is what the word names.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is red-shift caused by dust reddening the light on its journey?
items.correct: No. Red-shift is an increase in wavelength linked to the recession of the galaxy, not a change caused by material along the path.
items.misconception: The light passes through dust and loses energy on the way, which reddens it in the way a sunset is reddened.
items.why: Reddening by the atmosphere is a familiar everyday effect, and it offers a mechanism that seems to explain the colour word in the term. Reddening dims light without moving spectral lines. In red-shift the entire pattern of lines is displaced to longer wavelengths, and the size of that displacement grows with the distance and speed of the galaxy.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does light slow down over such a long journey, giving a longer wavelength?
items.correct: No. The increase in wavelength is due to the recession of the galaxy, not to the light losing speed.
items.misconception: Light gets tired over an enormous journey and slows down, and slower light must have a longer wavelength when it arrives.
items.why: Everyday moving objects slow down over long distances, and the idea is carried across to light without checking it. Light travels at the same speed through space however far it goes. What changes is the wavelength, and it changes because the source is receding.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a bigger red-shift mean a bigger or brighter galaxy?
items.correct: No. A bigger observed increase in wavelength means the galaxy is moving faster and is further away.
items.misconception: A large bright galaxy sends more light and so gives a bigger red-shift, so red-shift is really a measure of the size of the galaxy.
items.why: Bigger is taken to mean bigger in every sense, and the size of an effect is attached to the size of the object producing it. Red-shift is measured from the position of spectral lines, which does not depend on how big or bright the source is. The specification links a bigger observed increase in wavelength to greater speed and greater distance.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Every distant galaxy is receding from us. Are we at the centre of the universe?
items.correct: No. Any observer anywhere would see the same thing, because space itself is expanding everywhere.
items.misconception: If everything moves away from us in every direction then we must be standing at the centre of the expansion.
items.why: The only familiar way for things to move away in all directions is to be at the middle of an explosion, so a centre is assumed. When space itself stretches, the distance between every pair of galaxies grows, so any observer sees all the others receding and sees the more distant ones receding faster. No observation singles out a centre.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Did the Big Bang theory come from the supernova observations made since 1998?
items.correct: No. The theory was already established; the supernova observations refined what scientists say about how the expansion is changing.
items.misconception: The Big Bang theory came from the 1998 supernova observations, since those are the observations the specification names.
items.why: It is the only date given in the section, so it is attached to the biggest idea in the section. Red-shift observations are the evidence that supports the Big Bang theory. The supernova observations made since 1998 onwards added the later finding that distant galaxies are receding ever faster.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Nobody witnessed the beginning of the universe. Does that make the Big Bang untestable?
items.correct: No. A theory is tested by whether its consequences match what is observed now, such as the red-shift of light from distant galaxies.
items.misconception: The Big Bang is just somebody's guess about the past, because nobody was there to see it and so it cannot be tested.
items.why: Testing is imagined as watching an event happen, so an event in the distant past seems to be beyond the reach of evidence. A theory is tested by the observations it leads us to expect. The Big Bang model accounts for the observed red-shift of light from most distant galaxies, and further observations continue to test and develop it.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are dark mass and dark energy two names for the same thing?
items.correct: No. They are given in the specification as two separate examples of what is still not understood about the universe.
items.misconception: Dark mass and dark energy both just mean the invisible stuff out in space, so the two terms can be swapped freely.
items.why: Both terms begin with the same word and both refer to something that cannot be seen, so they are collapsed into one idea. Dark mass concerns matter that is not seen directly, while dark energy is the name attached to the ever faster recession of distant galaxies. The specification lists them as two examples of what is not understood.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
